questions.question: Why should AI-Driven Testing and QA be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because AI-generated unit tests are inherently more thorough than hand-written ones
Because the code coverage percentage is the most reliable signal that a release is safe to ship
Because a single golden-case suite can replace ongoing risk weighting once it exists
Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — shared signals, controls, and decision rules — not the idea that generated tests are automatically thorough, that coverage percentage proves safety, or that a golden-case suite can replace human risk weighting.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, what actually let a claim-processing bug reach production despite all AI-generated tests passing?
options: A date-handling edge case slipped through, because the generated tests mostly covered happy paths, not risky logic
A race condition in concurrent claim submissions that the regression suite had never been configured to catch at all
A missing property test for money-impact scenarios, which the team had deliberately skipped that sprint
An external-dependency outage during the manual exploratory testing pass right before release
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening example is a claim-processing service where AI-generated tests were all green but missed a date-handling edge case, because the suite covered happy paths — not a race condition, a skipped property test, or a dependency outage.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for AI-Driven Testing and QA?
options: A fully automated test suite that requires no human review before merging
A single pass/fail score with no breakdown of the underlying risk signals
A list of every unit test the AI generated, sorted by execution time
A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact is a classroom planner that outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not a self-approving test suite, a single opaque score, or a raw dump of generated tests.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Property tests that check invariants across many generated inputs, not just fixed examples
Skipping property tests and golden cases because the generated suite was already green
Letting the AI decide unilaterally which edge cases matter, without a human risk review, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Treating high code coverage numbers as proof that a release is safe to ship
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include property tests that check invariants across generated inputs — the opposite of trusting an all-green AI-generated suite, letting the model pick edge cases unsupervised, or treating coverage numbers as proof of safety.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: Only when the team happens to be running an open-source model instead of a hosted commercial API
Only when the feature has a visually complex or unusually polished user interface
Never — every AI-assisted testing scenario can stay an informal awareness exercise
When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as money impact are all running high
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, risk-heavy scenarios need a launch gate regardless of whether the model is open-source, the UI is polished, or the team would prefer to keep things informal.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To formally replace the project owner's sign-off on every single release decision
To keep the underlying risk assumptions hidden from the non-technical stakeholders on the team
To create a reusable worksheet or prompt that teams can keep applying after the course ends
To automatically generate completion certificates for participants once the workshop ends
questions.explanation: The output template is meant to become a reusable worksheet or prompt teams keep using after the course — not a substitute for the owner's sign-off, a way to hide assumptions, or an automatic certificate generator.
